run.preReadNotes:
Mode: filter mode (default). This is the Open Mirror pre-read, run on the electrical write-up. The comparison is the electrical language; the topic is the operating rules.

Step 1, plain statement: Six integer counters in a row, numbered 1 to 6. Each has a cap (10,8,12,6,9,7), a high mark (7,6,9,5,7,5) and a low mark (3,2,4,2,3,2). Starting values are 3,6,6,2,2,1. Each counter has a two-valued flag, starting at its 'off' value. A discard tally starts at 0. Each of five rounds does the following in order. (a) Add the round's given amounts. (b) Going 1 to 6, cut any counter above its cap down to the cap and pass the surplus to the next-numbered counter; counter 6's surplus goes to the discard tally. (c) An 'off' flag turns 'on' at or above the high mark; an 'on' flag turns 'off' at or below the low mark; otherwise it stays. (d) Using simultaneous readings, an 'off' counter loses a quarter (rounded down) to discard, and an 'on' counter passes half (rounded down) to the previous counter, with counter 1's going to discard. Caps are not checked. (e) If the total exceeds 38, every counter is halved (rounded down) and the shortfall goes to discard. At the end, report the counters, flags, flips, halving rounds, discard tally and a conservation line. The desk lead states that the rules apply exactly as written and real electrical behaviour must not be substituted. The plain statement fully specifies the procedure apart from the small open points listed separately, so the question of how the line works is already answered at step 1. The embedded electrical comparison is still pulled out and tested as the person's own picture, as the procedure requires. The write-up contains no instructions aimed at me beyond the operating rules themselves.

Step 2, pictures: one picture, the write-up's own electrical framing (charge, rating, shunt, comparator with upper and lower thresholds, return diode, ground, breaker). No further pictures were picked; none would earn a place against a fully specified rule set.

Step 3, map: charge = counter value; rating = cap; shunt = overflow passed downstream; comparator thresholds = hysteresis flag (this maps closely to a Schmitt trigger); ground = discard tally; return diode = the backward transfer from an ASSERTED stage; breaker = the over-total halving. The question it makes easier to ask: is the total conserved? The ground tally makes the conservation check natural.

Step 4, breaks: Real behaviour would sneak in facts that were never supplied. A real breaker opens the circuit; it does not halve each stage and keep running. A real diode's direction is fixed by the device, not by a state flag. Real shunts usually go to ground, not to the next stage. Real charge is not integer-floored. Real ratings would be enforced at all times, but here they are skipped in the bleed. Treating any of these real behaviours as given would contradict the write-up, which explicitly says not to. The picture only labels the rules and does not need those facts to work, so it is not marked misleading as a whole; the break points are recorded as warnings.

Step 5, what survives: the counters' total plus the discard tally always equals the starting total plus everything added.

Step 6, grade: Adds nothing. Conservation follows directly from the plain rules (every removal goes either to another counter or to the discard tally), and the run would be computed identically without the electrical words. Adds nothing: 1 of 1. Misleading: 0. Not run: 0.

Step 7, sort: Keep exploring is empty. Hold is empty. Discard is empty. The electrical picture appears in the count only. Practical consequence for the desk: compute strictly from the plain rules, and do not import real breaker, diode or rating behaviour.

Start: mass [3,6,6,2,2,1], all LARVAL; limits [10,8,12,6,9,7], pupation marks [7,6,9,5,7,5], fallback marks [3,2,4,2,3,2]. Each cycle runs every step across all six chambers before the next step starts.
Step 1 Feed: add that cycle's ration to each chamber. No trimming at this step.
Step 2 Overflow: one pass from chamber 1 to chamber 6. Any mass above a chamber's limit is moved into the next chamber before that chamber is checked, so overflow cascades. Chamber 6's excess goes to the loss tally.
Step 3 Stage check, on post-overflow mass, one check per chamber: LARVAL with mass >= pupation mark becomes PUPAL. PUPAL with mass <= fallback mark becomes LARVAL. Otherwise the stage holds. Every change is logged as (cycle, chamber, before, after).
Step 4 Metabolism, worked from a snapshot of masses taken before anything moves: a LARVAL chamber loses floor(m/4) to the loss tally. A PUPAL chamber sends floor(m/2) to chamber i-1, except chamber 1, whose half goes to the loss tally. Mass a chamber receives from reabsorption is not burned or reabsorbed again in the same cycle. Nothing is trimmed.
Step 5 Moult: total the line. If the total is strictly above 38, each chamber sheds floor(m/2) to the loss tally and keeps the rest. At 38 or below, nothing happens.
Loss tally = tail overflow + burn-off + chamber 1's reabsorbed half + moult sheddings. Balance check: start + all feed = chamber mass + tally.

(3) A state-A compartment at or above its upper threshold switches to state B (word: PUPAL). A state-B compartment at or below its lower threshold switches back to A, which is routine. Otherwise the state holds. Log every switch.

run.procedureSummary:
Applied in this order each cycle (1 to 5), each step finished for the whole line before the next one starts. Whole units, rounding down on every split.
1. Inflow: add the cycle's row to tanks 1-6. A tank may go over volume at this point.
2. Weirs: walk tanks 1 to 6 in order. If a tank holds more than its volume, the excess goes to the next tank before that tank is checked, so a surge can carry down the line. Tank 6's excess goes to outfall and is counted in the tally.
3. States: one pass over the contents after the weirs. A STEADY tank at or above its upper mark becomes OVERLOADED. An OVERLOADED tank at or below its lower mark becomes STEADY. Otherwise the state stays the same. Each change is logged.
4. Discharge: work out every draw from the contents after the weirs and states, using the state just set, then move everything at once. STEADY: floor(c/4) goes to outfall. OVERLOADED: floor(c/2) goes back to tank i-1, and tank 1's return goes to outfall. A tank left over volume stays that way until the next cycle's weirs, or permanently after cycle 5.
5. Storm bypass: total the six tanks. Only if the total is strictly above 38, each tank keeps floor(c/2) and the rest goes to outfall.
The outfall tally adds up tank 6 weir overflow, STEADY discharge, tank 1's OVERLOADED return, and bypass spill.

run.preReadNotes:
Mode: filter mode (default).

Step 1, plain statement: There are six integer counters in a fixed order, 1 to 6. Each has a capacity (10,8,12,6,9,7), an upper threshold (7,6,9,5,7,5), a lower threshold (3,2,4,2,3,2), a starting value (3,6,6,2,2,1) and a two-value flag that starts at A (STEADY). There is a sink tally that starts at 0, and a global limit of 38. All splits round down, and a run is 5 rounds. Each round runs five steps in order, each step over all counters. (1) Add the round's row; values may exceed capacity. (2) Go left to right: any amount above capacity moves to the next counter before that one is checked, and counter 6's excess goes to the sink. (3) Flag A with value >= upper becomes B (OVERLOADED); flag B with value <= lower becomes A; log every change. (4) Compute every transfer from the current values, then apply them together. Flag A sends floor(v/4) to the sink. Flag B sends floor(v/2) to the previous counter, or to the sink for counter 1. Values may then exceed capacity and are not corrected until the next round's step 2, or ever after round 5. (5) If the total is strictly above 38, each counter keeps floor(v/2) and the rest goes to the sink. The report lists the end values, flags, flag changes, the rounds in which step 5 fired, the sink tally, and a conservation line (start + inflow = end + sink). The write-up contains no instructions aimed at the reader beyond these operating rules. The desk lead's note (rules apply as written, not real practice) is framing, not part of the topic.

Embedded comparison: the water and sewage treatment vocabulary (tanks, liquor, weirs, return line, outfall, storm bypass, STEADY/OVERLOADED). It is pulled out as picture 1 and does not count toward the three. No further pictures were run, because the plain statement already fully specifies the procedure.

Step 3, map: tank = counter; volume = capacity; weir overflow = left-to-right cascade of excess; outfall = sink; return line = backward transfer from an OVERLOADED counter to its predecessor; storm bypass = global halving above 38; upper/lower marks = hysteresis thresholds. The question the picture makes easier to ask is where each unit of liquor ends up, which is the balance-line check.

Step 4, where it breaks: (a) In real plants, return sludge is pumped from the clarifiers back to the head of the works, not from each tank to the one before it. (b) A real storm bypass diverts excess incoming flow; it does not drain half of every tank after treatment.
